title: He stole their hearts (2 Samuel 15:1–6)
hook: Absalom wins the people at the gate with flattery
carry: a kiss, a nod, a sigh

segments.voice: Yesterday Tamar said no, and was told to hold her peace. Your line was her story is told. Today, her brother Absalom stands at the city gate, smiling.

Early morning at the gate of Jerusalem. A farmer has walked in from his town with a dispute, a boundary line, a debt, a stolen animal, to bring it to the king. Before he reaches anyone official, a handsome young man steps out from beside the road. Where are you from? The farmer tells him. The young man hears his case and nods. Your matters are good and right, he says. Then he lowers his voice. But there's no one from the king to hear you.
screen: `DAWN AT THE GATE.` → `A MAN WITH A CASE.` → `YOUR MATTERS ARE GOOD AND RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The young man is Absalom. Since Tamar, a lot has happened. He waited, had Amnon killed, and fled. Years later he was allowed home, and his father kissed him. Now he gets a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him, and goes to work at the gate. Look at his method. He rises early and stands beside the road. He asks each person where they're from. He tells every one of them their case is good and right, with only one side in front of him, and says the king has no one to listen. Then he sighs aloud: oh, that I were made judge in the land! Anyone with a cause could come to me, and I'd give them justice. When someone bows to him, he won't allow it; he takes hold of them and kisses them. Every move is warm. Every move is aimed. The text sums it up: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." The same Hebrew phrase, to steal a heart, appears in Genesis when Jacob slips away from Laban without telling him, and there it means fooling him. So the line has two edges: Absalom won their affection, and he did it by fooling them. He doesn't lie about everything. Maybe the courts really were slow. Maybe people really did feel unheard. He takes a real grievance and makes himself the answer, and he never has to decide a single case. Saying yes to everyone is easy when you never have to rule.
screen: `A CHARIOT AND FIFTY RUNNERS.` · `YOUR CASE IS GOOD AND RIGHT.` · `OH THAT I WERE MADE JUDGE.` · then, large: `HE STOLE THEIR HEARTS.` · then: `JACOB AND LABAN: THE SAME PHRASE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days to a moment when someone told you exactly what you wanted to hear, an ad, a voice online, a friend who agreed a little too fast, and ask the farmer's question: did they hear the other side? Then turn it around, gently, to a moment when you said only what someone wanted to hear; no need to judge it, just see it clearly.
Lev. The Hebrew word for heart, the thing Absalom quietly stole from the men of Israel. Today's word.
Your line: a kiss, a nod, a sigh. Warmth can be aimed. Day seven hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Jews read Absalom at the gate as part of the book of Samuel, and later Jewish teaching uses a related phrase, genevat da'at, stealing the mind, for misleading someone.
